utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today, we are Tuesday, the 20th of May, 2008. I would like to greet the witness. I would like to greet the OTP, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us. The Prosecutor must finish his examination-in-chief. You have half an hour left, so I shall give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Alic. Mr. Alic, last week we addressed various --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is really an outrage. The Prosecutor says, "Good morning," to the Trial Chamber, to Mr. Alic, and nothing to me, he says nothing to me. Well, is that the way to behave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to say hello to everyone, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what Mr. Dutertre said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Last week, we addressed your personal history, the forces in Zvornik in 1991 and 1992, the various political forces in Zvornik during this period, the military forces present around Zvornik, the most salient events which you remembered between October 1991 and April 1992, presented to you in a chronological order, when possible. And, lastly, the arrest of four Serbs in April 1992. That's what we were talking about when we left off last week, and we addressed in detail the situation of the two first men, the Vuckovic brothers. You clearly told us that they both had membership cards of the SRS and the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I would like to address the issue of the membership cards of the SRS. You mentioned this in 1996 already, and you mentioned that these people had these cards. Do you remember having testified in Belgrade in 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness never spoke about the IDs of the Serbian Radical Party in 1996, but exclusively of the Chetnik Movement. He started speaking about the IDs of the Serbian Radical Party in the proofing session, as the Prosecutor told me in the minutes from that proofing session, so the Prosecutor must not use that. And I'm going to prove, using that, that this witness is giving false testimony, because neither in 1996 or 1997 was there a membership card of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the use of the word, false witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're going so fast that it's difficult for us to keep up. And you talked about false witnesses, but there are intervals in the middle which haven't been addressed. I'm trying to understand when you talk about a false witness, and I'm trying to understand what the Prosecutor would like to establish. According to what I've understood, the witness testified in Belgrade in 1996, I believe. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say is that last week the witness explained to us that in 1996, he had told the investigator that these two cases existed. Then I started addressing the testimony of this gentleman in Belgrade in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor is telling us that in 1996, the witness had spoken to the investigator about these two cards, the Chetnik Movement card and SRS card.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, correct two cases by two cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... since he does not know how this was translated, because you yourself highlighted this on a several of occasions. We have your statements, ones you made to the investigators, and these are signed in English. And since the witness does not speak English, he may not have been made aware of the accuracy of his words translated into English as concern these two cards. And it's on this particular issue that the Prosecutor would like to get back to, since he seems to have addressed this during his testimony in 2006. Is that right, Mr. Dutertre? Have I got it right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hadn't addressed this last point yet, but this is exactly what I wanted to get at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how things stand. Mr. Seselj, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is impermissible for the Prosecutor to tell the witness that in 1996, "In the statement to the Prosecution, you said that two membership cards existed, the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement." That's how the Prosecutor began, so I assume you have that in the transcript, and that is impermissible. And if you look at both those statements, you will see that no mention is made of the membership cards of the Serbian Radical Party, but only of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. The first time that the witness mentioned the membership card of the Serbian Radical Party was at the proofing session which was held several days ago. Never before did he mention that. And I received the minutes from the proofing session. It is in three parts, and it is only there that the witness first mentions the Serbian Radical Party. So why is my objection well founded? Because the Prosecutor must not lead the witness and suggest that he said in 1996 something that the witness did not say at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, I believe that Mr. Seselj has -- is right at least on one point. The statement of 1996, which I have before me --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to what the witness told us last week as regards the statements he made in 1996. I'm not referring to the written statement of 1996, but the explanations provided by the witness as regards what he said in 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Dutertre, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what the witness said, and it is on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you give us the transcript page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can find it again, if you would allow me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the Prosecutor is looking for that, I'd like to draw your attention, Judges, to the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 7012, Your Honour, 7012, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7012.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19 to 25, lines 19 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar bring up this page, please. In the meantime, Mr. Seselj will address another issue. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is now telling you something new that I wasn't challenging at all. It is correct that last week, the witness mentioned two IDs or membership cards, that of the Serbian Radical Movement and the Serbian Chetnik Movement, but there's none of that in the 1996 statement, so this is quite impermissible behaviour. He can score a point with people that have an IQ at the level of idiots, but at this kind of level, you can't pull a fast one like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the transcript before me now, and I'm reading it on my colleague's screen. He explained it, on line 20, that the cards existed. That is the truth. One of the cards mentioned "SCP," and the other card "SRS," Serbian Radical Party. So he mentioned two cards here in the courtroom, whereas in the 1996 statement, only one card was mentioned. So, Witness, 15 years later, how is it that your memory has --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in 1996, it may sound ambiguous, but what I -- my point today, which was by way of introduction, I was just saying that the witness did state this at the time, and I was only quoting his words. Line 19 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. My colleague does not seem to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a problem for me, particularly in the light of what the Prosecutor said just a few moments ago. On line 2 -- on page 2, line 13, 14, 15 and 16, I don't know if it's a translation issue. Maybe it would be best to check what the Prosecutor said in French. It seems that he refers to something which the witness would have said to the investigator in 1996, as regards a membership card of the SRS. So we should check this. Did you actually say this, because if you have said this, I believe that the accused is right to object, because in the 1996 statement mention is made to a card of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and not the SRS, so let's be quite clear about this. This does not mean that the accused needs to be that aggressive when he objects. He could be perhaps a little bit more courteous, but basically he is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to what the witness said last week, and in these lines from 19 to 25, maybe I didn't express myself properly. But in these lines 19 to 25, he mentioned having mentioned it, and he said there might have been a translation problem at the time, I mean. This is why I did not mention the 1996 document, but I talked about what he had said in 1996. So maybe I didn't -- maybe I misspoke, but I was referring to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 19 of page 7012 in the English we have before us, we can read as follows, and he refers to both cards, and he even adds: [In English] "That is the truth." [Interpretation] So since there is an objection, I shall take charge of this. Now, we have the proof, Witness, that in 1996, in the English version -- normally speaking, the English version should match the B/C/S version, which I do not have. I do not have it. You only talked about one ID card of the Chetnik Movement, a membership card of the Chetnik Movement, and last week you said that in your statement, you mentioned two cards. So can you tell us what you actually said in 1996 to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said exactly that two different membership cards existed. I had them, I looked at them. I had them in my hands, I read them, and it is true, there were two different membership cards, one of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the other the Serbian Radical Party. So that is correct. Now, how that was translated, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're a professional. If that had been very important and if the investigator felt it was very important, why didn't you make sure that this was properly translated at the time, that this be really recorded on the transcript, because in your interview, this doesn't show. One has the feeling that these were cards of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I responded to the questions they asked me at the time, and that's what I said at the time; what I've just said now. Now, how it was translated and then written down, I don't know. I didn't look at all that, the translation of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the Prosecution provided you subsequently with the 1997 statement of this witness, so that you can see that on page 7, that he is talking about the same question, and he says that two brothers had membership cards issued by Seselj's paramilitary, para-army. So there's no mention of the Serbian Radical Party. This could bring to mind the Serbian Chetnik Movement, if the witness considers that to be my paramilitaries, but there was no Serbian Radical Party there even in 1997, and it doesn't exist in his Belgrade statement, in the Belgrade testimony. I don't know whether the Prosecutor has provided you with a copy of that, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one year later, the investigator of the OTP interviews you once again, and then something crops up. You talk about Seselj's paramilitaries, without mentioning the Serbian Radical Party. How can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to repeat for the umpteenth time, two different membership cards existed. Both of them were Seselj's paramilitary formations, both, because it wasn't the legal army ever. So both the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party, they were paramilitary formations, and it was one and the same formation, Seselj's one, but they had two different membership cards. The first membership card was produced much earlier, and according to some information it was banned over there, and then they opted for a different method, to use a milder expression for their party, and called it the "Serbian Radical Party." That's the truth of it, and I had those membership cards in my hands. I read them, and it cannot be otherwise. Now, how it was translated over there, I really can't explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and then I shall give the floor back to the Prosecutor. How would you define a paramilitary, according to your training? What is a paramilitary formation, in your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the forces who -- which were established, which were formed on the basis of certain people's volition, voluntarily, outside -- institutions outside the legal formations, and I said last time the legal formations were just the formations and units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Ministry of the Interior. All the rest were beyond, outside the system, which means paramilitary, illegal ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dutertre, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would just like to note that the translation of what I said, page 7, line 9, is incomplete. I shall not correct it now. I'd like time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember you testified in 2006?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember having mentioned the existence of these two cards, one card of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and one card of the SRS, the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In this trial in Belgrade in 2006, Mr. Seselj was not one of the accused, was he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, objection. I think that the Prosecutor must show you now that portion of the transcript from the Belgrade trial where this witness referred to those two membership cards. You can't just skip over that. He is relating to an exhibit, and now he must provide it. I will provide it during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it's on Mr. Seselj's time, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "If it's not on my time, that's fine." At the time you put the question, I thought you were going to show the witness a question which was put in Belgrade to the witness and his answer. I thought you were going to show him that to put it in context, because it's important to know what question this related to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document 7227 65 ter list page 627. I'm interested in the two pages here in B/C/S, so pages 7 and 8 have been translated, and other two pages have not been translated, but I can quote this. The Judge was asking --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor repeat the page number, because I omitted to hear one of the digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj. The translation in English is in the document. I can read it out, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Seselj to be able to check, we should show this on the screen. We should show the document, 7227.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, he did say "7227."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in B/C/S, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to read it to save time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness Asim Alic, there were two of them, identification cards, Seselj's members, one identification card, these were radicals, and before that there were -- I remember it well, identification cards labelled -- it said 'SCP' Serbian Chetnik identification card, military one, and it was on those grounds that I started contemplating --" No, sorry, sorry. [Interpretation] I've made a mistake, sorry: [In English] "... movement, and I know they were banned under a particular name, but the identification cards were still with them, so it gave me evidence of the [indiscernible] and whom they belonged to." [Interpretation] Is that what you stated in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I have an objection. First of all, the Prosecutor did not read out exactly what it says in the Belgrade statement, because I have page 7 in front of me of the original transcript of the 10th of March, 2006. The president of the Trial Chamber says: "Who was that?" That's on page 7. And the witness, Asim Alic, says: "They were two of them. Two of them had ID cards, Seselj's members, one ID card --" 1

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could ask the witness to read the translation out. I read the translation which I had, but maybe it would be best if the interpreters translate when Mr. Alic reads out this passage. Could we scroll down to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before you, you have the text in B/C/S of the hearing. Clearly, a question is put by the judge and the witness answers. Clearly, we are dealing with a professional judge here, because the questions are extremely professional. Could you read out the answer you gave, which is in B/C/S here? With that, the interpreters can translate what you are reading out to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They were -- two people had them, had identification cards, Seselj's members. One of the IDs, those were the Radicals, and before them, I remember well, IDs that were called -- on them, it said 'the SCP,' the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and I know that what it was under that name that they were prohibited, but they still had those IDs. So that was proof even more of their affiliation, to whom they belonged." It is true I said that, but look at the second sentence in that paragraph: "They were people. They had identification cards. Seselj's members, one identification card said 'the Radicals,' so I'm talking about one where it said the Radicals and one where it said the Serbian Radical Party. One was the Chetniks and the other the Serbian Radical Party, but it is true that there were two. And I clearly spoke about the two of them. I clearly saw them, and that's the truth of it."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we've just heard the translation of what you've said. The important point is the beginning. I would like you to read this out again slowly, please, just the beginning. So read it again, and read it slowly so that the interpreters can do their job properly. So please read it out again, just the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They were people -- two people had identification cards. When I say 'identification cards,' I mean several. He didn't have one. It's not in the singular, it's in the plural. I remember well the identification cards were called -- on it, it said --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness is now doing has no sense. The witness isn't reading, he is interpreting it subsequently and interpreting it wrongly. You asked the witness to read it out, so the witness has to read it out word by word without any comments. You can ask for comments later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, can you please read what is in the text, but word for word? Mr. Seselj speaks the same language that you do, so if there is a difference, he will object. So please start again from the beginning, without commenting anything. Just read out loud what is written on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They were -- they were two people that had -- they had ID cards, Seselj's members, one ID card that was those Radicals, and before that there were, I remember that well, ID cards that were called -- it said on them 'SCP,' the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and I know that they were banned under that name, but those ID cards were left, and that was proof even more of their affiliation of who they belonged." And then it says, the next sentence: "Double, they had double." That's what I said in my testimony, they had double IDs, and that's what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the beginning of the text read by the witness, there is a reference. He says there were two men. They had ID cards, Seselj's men, and the translation says one ID card, they were Radicals. So in the first part of the sentence, it does not seem that -- at least not formally that there was one ID card from the Serbian Radical Party. At least this is what I heard through the translation. However, at the end of the sentence, one could think that there were two ID cards. But it's not clear at all when you read the first part of the sentence. Mr. Prosecutor, this being said, you can now have the floor and proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the interpretation you received was not correct. The correct one is: "Those were." There were two people. They had ID cards, Seselj's members. So the witness is speaking in disjointed sentence. "One ID," that's those Radicals, and not those were the Radicals, so you get a wrong translation. That was a reinterpretation of what was just said in French. It says: "Those were the Radicals," so the witness gives a broader explanation, but please look at what it says in the paragraph below, three lines down. The witness says: "I remember -- I remember that of the two that belonged to the Serbian Chetnik Movement or to the Radicals ..." So he identifies the Serbian Chetnik Movement with the Radicals, and he's not talking about the Radicals' IDs. He says those who had IDs of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, those were Radicals, in his opinion. That's the essence, in his view. And then he goes on to explain what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the first translation that we heard, what was said was they were Radicals, and Mr. Seselj is telling us that this is wrong, it was these were his Radicals. So there's a difference between these were Radicals and these were his radicals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thank Mr. Seselj for all his -- I already read this translation, we can ask for a new translation of this passage for confirmation. This is the translation I obtained. I can only quote from this translation, I can't do anymore. The witness gave us his explanation regarding this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is asking the CLSS to translate in French and English the passage in question, read by the witness in his own language. Let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, please, did you ask Repic, the younger brother, whether he was a member of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did he answer?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He replied in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that he also had a membership card of the Chetnik Movement. Did you know at that time who headed this movement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who was it, please?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was Mr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ulemek is one of the four people who happened to be at the Public Security Station that day. He was a member of the paramilitary formations run by Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did you know he was a member of the paramilitary formations run by Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We found several ID cards on Ulemek. One of them was the military ID card, the regular card ID card of the Yugoslav People's Army. The other ID card -- or another ID card was that of Arkan's Tigers, and the third one was that of the French Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On the card of Arkan's Tigers, was there a photograph, his photograph?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was a photograph, and he himself confirmed in his statement that he belonged to Arkan's paramilitaries and that he had in his possession the ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I've said earlier, he had a number of ID cards, but there was the same name and the same photograph certified by a stamp in all of them, and that was Miroslav Ulemek, Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What does "Legija" mean?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Legija was his nickname. I think he probably got this nickname because he belonged to the French Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What is Ulemek doing at the moment; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that Ulemek is currently serving his sentence which was confirmed on appeal in a Serbian prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know why he was convicted?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was charged with several offences, including the assassination of the Serbian Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I believe that there might be a problem at line 17, page 25. You talk about Milorad Ulemek or Miroslav Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Milorad, Milorad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the fourth man arrested on the same day?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The fourth man was also a member of Arkan's paramilitaries, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was Zvezdan Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is the person called "Stojanovic"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's the one, that's the person. On two or rather three occasions that I gave statements, and it is possible that I had made a mistake, a slip of a tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. You said he was a member of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, it is not clear, what the witness is affirming now, whether it is Zvijezda Novanovic or Zvijezda Stojanovic, the fourth man. Let us see what is the final statement made by this witness. I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please give us some details of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I was not 100 per cent certain about the last name, but I am 100 per cent certain about this man, because he was present at the Public Security Station the whole day, and I spoke to him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I could refresh the witness's memory on this. Referring to his hearing, his interview of July 13, 1996, page 4, paragraph 18 -- if you may, I'll read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. This is authorised by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you: [In English] " ... second arrested man was Stojanovic, a dentist from Belgrade, who had Arkan's ID card as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this what you said in 1996, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated, and that was recorded as my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier, you said that these four men, Repic, Zuto, Ulemek and now Stojanovic were going to the is that Jezero Hotel in Mali Zvornik. Did they tell you the names of the people they were supposed to meet at the Jezero Hotel in Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. They had the intention to go to the Jezero Hotel, but they never got there, because they made a mistake and they crossed the Drina River to the right bank into Bosnia sooner than they were expected, and that's why they never did establish this contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. But who were they supposed to meet at the Jezero Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, they spoke about several people there. The one of those persons that was supposed to be there was Arkan, and there was also Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what Arkan did before the war?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I could only speculate, and I'm not here to speculate. I heard that he was a pastry maker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said that Repic and Zuto had been mentioned as having -- as authors by people who were rescued from camps that had been set up around Zvornik. Was Ulemek also mentioned by these people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What about Stojanovic, was he also mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. All four were mentioned, and a specific detailed description was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You also said that on the Serbian side, there had been phone calls in order for these four men to be released from the Zvornik police station. Among these four men, was there one which the Serbians seemed to be more -- feel more important?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were several phone calls made on that day. Of course, I was not in contact over the phone with that person. That was done by my colleague, but he briefed me regularly and he relayed to me the demands made by the other side. The other side insisted on the surrender of all four, but the stress was placed on Ulemek, Legija. Since Legija held the military ID card of the regular Yugoslav People's Army among the ID cards that he had, with the military post codes that corresponded to the Pancevo military police, at first I wanted to call the military police and to hand him over to them, because I thought he was a military policeman, but it was just one of the ID cards that he had in order to identify himself and to ensure free passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done with my question, but I would like one thing to be clarified, if I may. In the transcript, page 6970, line 12, there may be a problem with the translation here. I said: [In English] " ... against Dragan Spasojevic aided the SDS in Zvornik, do you mean that he was a chairman?" [Interpretation] I would like to know whether this is a mistake or whether we are really talking about Mr. Brano Grujic as head of the SDS in Zvornik, rather than Dragan Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, the president of the Serbian Chetnik Movement in Zvornik was Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question. If I understood you well, these four people, according to you, two were linked to the Chetnik Movement, possibly to Seselj's men. The third one, Ulemek, has a membership card from Arkan's, and the fourth one, the dentist, Stojanovic, seems also to be in the same movement as Arkan. These four individuals were arrested by chance because they lost their way, and you hear them, you interview them, and it seems that they were supposed to meet someone at the Jezero Hotel in Mali Zvornik. They were supposed to meet two people, actually, Arkan and Grusic [as interpreted]. Grusic is the head in Zvornik of a party, but it is not the Serbian Radical Party. Is it exactly what you were said? Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may help you, it's Grujic, not Grusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So these four people were supposed to meet someone who was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party. Is this what happened; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you found out that this meeting was to be held, did you try and find out what was the purpose of the meeting, why the meeting had been set up? What seems quite surprising is that these four individuals were dressed like Rambo. They had the entire gear, you know. They were geared up like people who wanted to carry out some kind of military action. So did you ask them what they were supposed to do at that hotel, what was the purpose of the meeting, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day, I asked them a series of questions. Among the questions I asked was the question that you just mentioned. They said that they had come with the intention of helping and protecting the Serb people in Zvornik, and I said, "What kind of help are you offering?" And they said, "The Serb people is under threat in Zvornik, it is threatened by Muslims. The Muslims are mistreating them, killing them, raping them, and we are here to help them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this meeting seemed to have been organised by Arkan and this Grujic, and the purpose was to protect Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the meeting was organised by Mr. Grujic and that Arkan and all the others were the paramilitaries. They were mercenaries, they were looters, and they gladly responded to such summons because they were bound to get a lot of money and a lot of the looted property, and they were doing that on a large scale at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you can start the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj, you have two and a half hours, and you may proceed. You have the floor, and we will have our break around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, since you worked as a police officer in Belgrade and you were a member of the city brigade of the police, did you ever meet me in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kinds of meetings were they?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the most part, you often stood in front of the Federal Assembly with a loudspeaker, and you made those inflammatory speeches, and for the most part you had around you your entourage of followers and the passersby, who would stop and look at you, and would cause disturbance to the traffic. And it was our brief to make sure that the traffic flowed freely, and we had to remove you from that area in order to ensure that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in order to remove me, you had to arrest me?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if that's the term that you're using. Let me explain what we did. We removed you, we put you in an official vehicle, and we took you to the 29th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges what the 29th November is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's the unit of the Ministry of the Interior, where the custody area was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many times did you arrest me in this manner?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, quite a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, sometimes once or twice daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many times in total?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, at the minimum, 10 or 15 times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It is very easy, when you both speak the same language, to just rattle off in a conversation. That, however, leaves the interpreters as well as the Judges, and probably also the Prosecutor, completely outside your very interesting conversation. I therefore kindly ask you to respect a pause, and I don't know if the best way for you, Mr. Witness, is to count to five before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in 1990 and 1991, you took part in arresting me several times. And in your statement dated 1997, it says that you did it 10 or 20 times, perhaps more?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, Mr. Alic, we had skirmishes before. This is not the first one. I'm intrigued by something you said in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. At the time, you know, Mr. Seselj, did he have some kind of a mandate? Was he a member of parliament or what? I'm asking this question, because if he was a member of parliament, he must have had some kind immunity. You can't arrest a member of parliament like that, so I'd like to know exactly what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew at the time who we could arrest and who we couldn't arrest. At that time, Mr. Seselj was nothing but the president and the founder of a party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was arrested while I was a member of the parliament. I came here from the Federal Parliament, so all those stories about immunity had nothing to do with anything. I actually arrested myself when I was a member of the Federal Parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Contrary to what you've been saying, Mr. Seselj says he'd been elected, so obviously there's a difference in terms of substance. You were part of the police force, so you were supposed to know the law. At the time, do you know whether a member of parliament could be arrested? Was it possible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the law, it was not possible, but I doubt that he had any kind of immunity, because if he had immunity and if we made that mistake the first time, we couldn't have made that mistake the 20th time, because by that time we would already know that he had immunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps he needs some additional information. I became a member of the parliament in July 1991, and Mr. Alic testified that he left Belgrade in October, so that was a couple of months before I became. But let me remind you that I was arrested in 1994 and 1995, when I had immunity, and I was kept in custody for a long time. But that's immaterial. What is important to me is what Mr. Alic said in his examination-in-chief, and that is that I was supposed to visit Bratunac in early 1992, but that the arrival was postponed because strong forces had arrived from Tuzla and they were getting ready to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that what you stated, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to know whether Mr. Seselj could quote the page of the transcript he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the transcript has not been translated into Serbian, and you know that you're not translating it into Serbian but you're just giving me DVDs, and it takes my team a month or more to transcribe it, to put it on paper. And instead of being ashamed of what you're doing to me, you're now taunting me with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you cannot give a positive answer to this request because the transcript is not in B/C/S. Therefore, you cannot answer this request. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think there's anything that is challenged there. I assume you remember the witness saying that, and he's just confirmed this. And as this is new, as far as I'm concerned, I'd never heard about it before, that's the question I began with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, this happened sometime at the beginning of 1992, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was supposed to go to Bratunac, and then the special police came from Tuzla to arrest me; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You were supposed to be present in Bratunac and to deliver some of your speeches there, and we had information according to which you would arrive, you would be arriving and crossing over into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, your arrival could have caused an upset in inter-human relations more than was already the case, and we wanted to prevent that. We wanted to prevent that, and we would have prevented it by arresting you. That's a fact, we would have arrested you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what would you have done with me then?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't make the decisions. Somebody above me would have made those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how could you arrest someone for preventative reasons without that person having committed a crime at all?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There is a way to do that, to arrest people without them having committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ah, well, that's what I wanted to hear from you, those ways of arresting people without them having committed any crime. Very well, Mr. Alic, I'm very grateful to you for adding to my biography, my CV, because I've never heard about that, but you said that the Security Service cautioned me and warned me that I was going to be arrested, and that's why I didn't go. So which service was it who warned me ?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to our information, because in our building, where the Public Security Station was located, there was a Department of State Security, too, so that's how.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that before that, anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina I held public rallies and made my political speeches; did you ever hear of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you. I had one in Bijeljina, in closed -- a closed premises, the Serbia Cafe, and in Banja Luka as well at the end of 1991, in passing through towards Western Slavonia, and you've heard of the Borik hall, I assume, in Banja Luka. But over there, we had already established the Serbian Radical Party there, both in Bijeljina and in Banja Luka, whereas in Zvornik and Banja Luka, we didn't have any -- in Bratunac. And you thought we did?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I don't deal with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you would have heard how the party existed; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you didn't hear about that. How could I then hold a rally in a place where the Serbian Radical Party doesn't exist at all? Who would have organised it for me? I assume you form a party first and then you go on to work for the party.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, somebody should have -- could have prepared the terrain for you so that you had sympathizers. The people hear of you, hear your speeches, and then become members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you have to set the groundwork for that, an initiative board or a municipal board, and then rally the people into membership; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj and the witness are talking together extremely fast, and it's very difficult to raise an objection. But obviously the witness is asked to speculate on a number of things. He said that he had heard about a party, and when checking his answers, you see that he's only speculating. So this is why I'm raising an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, given the objection that has just been raised, the important thing is the following: In Zvornik, was there, yes or no, presence of the Serbian Radical Party? You said, "I was not involved in politics." Fine, but this is not what you're asked. You were asked whether, as a policeman, you knew whether there was or whether there was not a Serbian Radical Party in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question, because I'm not quite sure whether it existed or not, but that sympathizers of the Serb Radical Movement did exist. I can say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Alic, in Tuzla there are many sympathizers of the Serbian Radical Party without a municipal board. There's no organisation there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. We may have a translation issue here. In French, I heard "there were representatives of the SRS," and after that I heard "sympathizers." It's not quite the same. So "sympathizers," the interpreter has just corrected this. According to you, there were sympathizers in Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "sympathizers," not "representatives," so sympathizers of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you said that you left Belgrade because in that police unit, and I'm paraphrasing now, there was a burgeoning nationalistic atmosphere and that your new commander, a Serb, Aleksandar Bosovic, ordered that in the brigade only Serbs should remain; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not. The then commander, Aleksandar Bosovic, was the commander up until that time, and he never said that. However, when he was replaced with his replacement, a new commander arrived and words like that were heard -- said by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm referring you to page 3 of your 1997 statement, and that -- and paragraph 3 of that page is what I'd like to refer you. You say: "At that time, our brigade received a new commander. He was a Serb, Aleksandar Bosovic, who ordered that all policemen from our brigade should only be Serbs. I attended a meeting at which he said that from now on, the brigade would be known as the Serb Guard. After I heard that terrible news, I decided that I was not going to stay in Belgrade at any cost and that I would return to Bosnia." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is true that I said that. However, I didn't say the name "Aleksandar Bosovic," because Aleksandar Bosovic was the commander up until that time, until that time, and he never made that statement. He was quite proper, a normal man, quite different from the other man who replaced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this is what it says in your statement. I didn't add that, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know what I said, but there might have been a mistake in the translation. So I state again and claim that that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Alic, there's no mistake in the translation. You signed each page of the Serbian personally, so you signed the Serbian version, not the French or the English. So there is no translation error. That's how you signed it in 1997, on page 3. Here's your signature, and your signature's on every page.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I know full well what I signed. I know very well what I stated. However, I claim and state that there is a mistake in the writing of the name and surname of the commander up until that time and from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, when you read this text --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there must be a mistake. On page 31, line 22, where Mr. Seselj says that the witness has signed the Serbian version, what I have before me is a version in English that is signed. I just wanted to specify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj has read out to you what you stated, and in what you said, Aleksandar Bosovic was the new commander, who said, "From now on, there will only be Serbs." Now you're saying that this is a mistake. So you made the mistake or is it the investigator who wrote this down and wrote the name down? But if it's the investigator who wrote the name down, he can only have written it down according to what you told him. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a mistake in the translation there, because Mr. Aleksandar Bosovic was the commander up until that time, which means that he was replaced at that point in time and a new commander arrived who made that statement, and that new commander is whom I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Alic signed the English version, too, but he quite certainly did sign the Serbian version, and here we have his signature. Now, on the second page of the statement, something was corrected here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. We need to start again because we didn't get the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to clarify this, in the proofing notes that were sent to Mr. Seselj, as far as this paragraph is concerned, something is being specified by the witness here, and he mentions --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely impermissible. This is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to quote some --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This deserves our attention. Mr. Seselj, please start again, put your question again, because we could not hear the interpretation when you were speaking. I think it's working again, so please repeat what you said when I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecutor said that Mr. Alic had signed the statement in English. Perhaps that is correct. I don't know. But what I can see is that he signed the statement in Serbian as well. On page 3 -- page 3 is where the paragraph that I quoted from is, and Mr. Alic's signature at the bottom. And we can show that in court here, if need be. Now, on the second page, we see here in paragraph 5 that Mr. Alic corrected something in his statement. What it said was this: "At the end of 1982, I graduated from the machine construction faculty." And then reading the statement, he crossed that out, because the word was "strojarstvo," which is a term he never used in his life, and then he corrected it and said, I graduated from the school of engineers for work organisation, and then you signed the correction. Again, you can see that on the screen, but I fear that this is going to take up too much time. Anyway, put this on the overhead protector, and you'll see how conscientious Mr. Alic was in correcting that and signing it, and now look at the other page that I quoted from and Mr. Alic's signature there, too. Then you can return the documents to me. And I hope that while we're waiting, this isn't deducted from my time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it might be useful to know when this version in B/C/S was signed, if we compare it with the English version which was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in your statement in your language, we have a written proof of this here, you may have made corrections. The first question: When were these corrections made; in 1996 or after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these were done straight away when I gave the statement, but probably in reading through the statement -- the rest of the statement, that I didn't happen to notice what Mr. Seselj is insisting upon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Give that back to me, then. That's enough. You didn't notice it; fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this -- when the statement, 92 bis, was signed, the first page mentioned that this was signed on the 24th of July, 2005. That's when the document was signed in the witness's own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- what's going on is quite unbelievable. The witness signed the statement of the 19th of May, 1997, in the Serbian version. Here you have his signature on page 1, on page 2, and here the corrections in his own hand, and here is page 3 from which I quoted, here is page 4, and every page is signed. So why don't you prevent the Prosecutor from using those methods? It's impermissible. This is the 1997 statement, and nowhere does it say "92 bis," so why don't you intervene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I step in when it's really worthwhile. When, at first hand, the consequences are nil or non-existence, then I don't, but in this case I think we should shed some light. Mr. Prosecutor, you talk about the 24th of July 2005 and you mention a 92 bis statement. If I understood you correctly, after this statement was written in 1996, you prepared a written statement, a 92 bis written statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a written statement which is a 92 bis statement, which was signed. I have the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it dated?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 26th of July, 2006, in Tuzla. This is what the representative of the Registry states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a statement dated 24th of July, 2005, which the Bench does not have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please, could you explain to me why I was not given that statement? I can understand why you weren't, maybe you don't need it, but why wasn't I provided this 24th of July, 2005 statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was disclosed to Mr. Seselj, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can let you know in the course of the morning, but I am positive this was disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was never disclosed to me. I've never seen it. Certainly, it wasn't disclosed to me, and I was preparing to ask those questions, because Mr. Asim Alic, on the 10th of March in Belgrade -- or, rather, 2006, he testified in Belgrade and stated on that occasion that the previous year, he gave some sort of statement to the Prosecution and that he gave two statements a year before that. That's what Mr. Alic said. So there are a total of three statements over a period of two years prior to the testimony in Belgrade, and I have received none of those statements, none of those three, and that is in the transcript of the Belgrade proceedings. Now, why wasn't I disclosed that? I think that that's quite unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Your Honour, all the statements made by the witness have been disclosed to the accused. I shall get back to you on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, Mr. Dutertre, that there were a lot of problems between Mr. Seselj and the previous Trial Chambers and the pre-trial Judges. These problems were due to the fact that he had been given a standby counsel. From then on, Mr. Seselj refused a whole series of documents. When I was asked to become the Pre-Trial Judge, I was asked to check this out, and I asked the Prosecutor to disclose to Mr. Seselj all those documents in a hard copy version, which -- and in his own language, as far as a witness which was a Prosecution witness, it is important that Mr. Seselj have all the documents, the 1996 statement, 1997, the written statements made in 2005, as well as the transcript pages of his testimony in Belgrade in 2006. So since this is a Prosecution witness, the accused should have received five documents, at the least. This is -- I don't know what the issue revolves around. The previous proceedings were a bit of a mess, but now we know where we stand, but we still have to deal with the adverse effects of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the transcript in Belgrade, this was a transcript on the 10th of March, 2008, number 275 in the 92 bis package, this was disclosed in several goes; on the 13th of May, 2008, 349 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly, Mr. Dutertre, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and 59, letter 59, on the 13th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can disclose this to Mr. Seselj and to the Bench. As soon as I have enough copies, I can distribute these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I insist on claiming that this has not been disclosed to me. And, Mr. President, you ordered, right at the beginning of the trial, that the Prosecution must prepare a full set of documents pertaining to that witness before he comes to testify, regardless of whether the documents have been disclosed at an earlier date or not. I remember that quite clearly, and the Prosecution is not meeting this obligation fully. It is disclosing documents that it chooses to. It should, however, provide all the documents in the folder for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, in the future for all Prosecution witnesses, please check that if a witness, X, Y or Z, has made or provided written statements, has testified, that all of this has been properly disclosed to Mr. Seselj and that you have the proof that he has received the documents, i.e., acknowledgment of receipt, to avoid any problem in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That will be done, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. In addition, Mr. Mundis, since you are here in the courtroom, I would like to impart to you something which the Trial Chamber wishes to see in the future. Mr. Ulemek, we discovered that this person was tried and convicted. This was something which was addressed during the hearing. We feel that we have insufficient information. We have not much knowledge about legal proceedings against some people who are mentioned in the statements provided by the witnesses, and the Trial Chamber would like to have all the documents that relate to these witnesses that have been tried in other cases. And there are two documents which are important; the indictment relating to them and the judgements, if judgements there are. In the case of Mr. Ulemek, for instance, who was part of the quatro that was arrested by this witness, I understand that he was incriminated in the assassination of the former prime minister. Therefore, it would be perfectly logical for the Bench to have these documents, i.e., the indictment against Ulemek and the judgement that convicted him, that sentenced him. We need to have this minimal information. You know that the Rules entitle us to do this. We shall turn to the Prosecution and ask it to complete this either by interviewing -- having the interview of Mr. Ulemek before the Trial Chamber that convicted him. We need to have at least the indictment and the judgement. That is the bare minimum that we are entitled to request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I take it from those remarks that the Chamber is calling for the production of this evidence, and we will file this material and make it available, and request that it be assigned exhibit numbers as soon as we're able to gather all the material and put it into a comprehensive filing, if you will, and we'll be submitting that for its submission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Also, disclose it to Mr. Seselj, if he doesn't have it yet. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you mentioned that on the 5th of April, there was an attack on a column -- on a JNA column in the village of Sapna and that one non-commissioned officer, a sergeant, was killed, and when the army returned fire, a villager from Sapna was also killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How was it, then?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the military column moving through Sapna opened fire first from the motor vehicles on the buildings, on the mosque. They opened fire in order to intimidate the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who returned fire?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's when the villagers of the Sapna village returned fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How? Did they fire from their own homes, from their doors and windows?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was not there to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So how could they just spontaneously return fire? The moment they hear gunfire, they just run to their windows, they grab their machine-guns, their rifles, and they open fire? Were they organised in order to be able to return fire, if indeed the army was the first to open fire, or did they just sporadically return fire as they grabbed their weapons? How was it, then, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing. This was not the first case where the army column would come and then the soldiers would open fire. Every single column moving from Usice, from Valjevo, as they passed through Mali Zvornik, as they crossed the bridge at Karakaj, I myself witnessed that. I was at the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, please do not waste my time. Let me just get from you what happened in Sapna. I'm not interested in the broad picture. You said that in Sapna, there was a clash between the army personnel and the people from Sapna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Mr. Seselj. You made a mistake when you asked the witness to only focus on Sapna. The witness is saying that this was common practice on the part of the army. When they arrived in an area, they started shooting. If that is a common practice, well, then, maybe this is what was done in this village. So this may stand to reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first clash that occurred in the territory of Zvornik was the one in the village of Sapna, and there is no logic to what the witness is trying to do now. That was the first clash. That was when the first casualties occurred, and that's where it all started. A JNA column was moving from Tuzla to Zvornik, and in the village of Sapna it was ambushed. There was gunfire directed at the column, and this warrant officer, a non-commissioned officer, was killed. The army personnel returned fire, and one of the villagers who took part in the ambush was also killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that when this clash occurred, that four or five soldiers went missing? Mr. Alic, you should know that. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, what you said earlier is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm not expecting you to be entirely honest. Let us move on. I said what I had to say. You said what you had to say. You, yourself, said you did not know that, that you were not in Sapna?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: But my sources of information say it the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, then tell me, how was it? The army personnel came in, they opened fire. How did the villagers respond spontaneously from the barns, they ran into their doorways, windows; how did they respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. The question by Mr. Seselj has been well put, so please answer the question. We can clearly see the situation. The JNA arrives in the village and something happens. So please tell us what you know about this, because Mr. Seselj has a theory which he is developing, in his eyes, and it's important also for the Trial Chamber. Before Zvornik, this incident occurred in Sapna, and according to his theory, the JNA fell in an ambush or was ambushed, so this is why he's putting this question to you. So please answer the question according to what you know. If you can't answer the question, do not speculate or misconstrue this. This is how the truth can emerge. Mr. Seselj, please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in the course of this clash, five JNA soldiers went missing, four or five, from that column? I cannot be more specific than that. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of the Tank Battalion, Captain Dragan Obrenovic, threatened that if the soldiers were not freed immediately, that he would raze Sapna to the ground?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that that very same Captain Dragan Obrenovic was tried here before this Tribunal; in the meantime, he was promoted to the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to ask you if you knew that he actually made a plea bargain with the Prosecution. But if you don't know that, we will not explore that with you. We will do that through other witnesses. So we will deal with Dragan Obrenovic in detail. Do you know that after that, the villagers of Sapna, the armed inhabitants of Sapna, handed over the four or five soldiers to the army?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you know that. And then on the next day, the 6th of April, did Colonel Tacic come to Zvornik and issue an ultimatum for the hand-over of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know that he came, and I personally escorted Colonel Tacic from the barricade to the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it the aim of his going there to ask for the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I did not attend the meeting. I don't know what was discussed, but I heard from the police chief, who did attend the meeting, that this was one of the topics discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your statement, at page 5, you said: "My chief informed me that the colonel had called him to talk about the hand-over of all the weapons on the part of the Zvornik authorities."

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were weapons handed over to Colonel Tacic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was an order earlier whereby the JNA seized all the weapons from the Territorial Defence, but the weapons that we're talking about were not handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since the weapons were not handed over, Colonel Tacic said that Zvornik would be attacked unless the weapons were handed over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was on the 6th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And on the 8th, there was this clash in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was no crash in Zvornik. There -- what happened was an attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if Serbs had to leave Zvornik because you had distributed weapons to a large number of criminals in Zvornik, and that made them feel insecure, well, then we can't talk about an attack on Zvornik, because the Serbs had moved out of Zvornik and then started off to reclaim -- recapture their town, and they had the support from the volunteers and the army?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not correct at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question or is Mr. Seselj testifying on what happened in Zvornik? Still, the witness said that weapons had been widely given to criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, the scenario could be the following, and here this is conditional: The JNA goes towards the village of Sapna. The JNA's ambushed. Obviously, something happened, because at first you didn't say anything, and then after a number of questions with Mr. Seselj, you agreed with him and said that four soldiers from the JNA had been captured by the villagers. Very well, but this is an armed column --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Armoured column," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can imagine the situation, and of course there will be negotiations, and these four soldiers are released. And the JNA finds out that the villagers are armed, and because of this, Colonel Tacic goes to Zvornik and officially asks for these weapons to be handed over, all weapons, and he poses an ultimatum in that respect. On the 8th, the ultimatum is actually implemented. This is the scenario put forward by Mr. Seselj, through his questions and through your answers. Now, we would like to know whether this assumption is possible, whether it's completely false. You were there, so what can you tell us about this? But tell the truth. We want the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there has been a swap of arguments here. The JNA column had free passage to go anywhere. It could not have been ambushed or trapped anywhere, because at that time the people still trusted the Yugoslav People's Army. But because there were those large-scale incidents wherever they passed, the people still tolerated that. They waited patiently for better times to come. When this column -- when columns passed through, they would always fire in the air, fire at mosques, at other buildings, in order to intimidate the people, in order to create some kind of a psychological effect in the people, insecurity, and it is a fact that the villagers of Sapna were armed, some of them. They had purchased the weapons, whereas the Serbs got their weapons from the Yugoslav People's Army. This was distributed to them in a systematic manner, with the police going house to house escorting a military truck from village to village, from house to house, leaving the weapons at the doorstep. On the other hand, Muslims had to buy weapons with their own money, and that's the truth. And they were armed, but to a lesser extent. Colonel Tacic issued this ultimatum, but only to one side, to the Muslim side. He asked them to hand over their weapons, whereas as far as Serbs were concerned, he actually provided weapons to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, how can you explain that four soldiers in a motorised column, maybe even an armoured column, were actually captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the shooting started, those soldiers jumped out of the trucks and they ran into the village, and they went to the first home that they encountered, and the people there took them in.
